messages.subject: Finite Mixture of Multivariate Normals
parts:
Dear all,

Firstly, congrats for your excellent work in Stan! 

I want to use HMC in order to fit a finite mixture model in which the distributions are not from the same family and 1 of them is parametrised for that specific problem. So, I came across Stan as an alternative to writing my own code. 

However, I have been trying to fit a simple finite mixture model for multivariate Normals but I am clearly missing something. More specifically, I simulate some data from 2 distributions and one of the mixing parameters goes to 1 and the other to 0 every time I run the script. The code with the generated data is the following:



mix_code="""
 data {
   int<lower=0> N; // number of individuals
   int<lower=1> D; // dimension of multivariate normal
   int<lower=1> K; //number of mixture distributions
   vector[K] alpha; // parameters of dirichlet prior for the theta
   matrix[N,D] y;  // outcomes
 }
 
 parameters {
   simplex[K] theta;
   matrix[K,D] mu;
   cholesky_factor_corr[D] L_Omega[K];
   vector<lower=0>[D] tau[K];  
 }

  transformed parameters{
   matrix[D,D] var_cov[K];
   for (m in 1:K){
     var_cov[m] <- diag_pre_multiply(tau[m],L_Omega[m]) * diag_pre_multiply(tau[m],L_Omega[m])';
   }
 }
 

  model {
   real ps[K];
   theta ~ dirichlet(alpha);
   for(m in 1:K) {
     // Priors for var-cov matrices and mu:
     tau[m] ~ cauchy(0,5);
     L_Omega[m] ~ lkj_corr_cholesky(D);
     mu[m]~normal(0,10);
   }
   
   for(n in 1:N) {
     for(m in 1:K) {
       ps[m] <- log(theta[m]) + multi_normal_log(y[n],mu[m],var_cov[m]);
     }
     increment_log_prob(log_sum_exp(ps));
   }
 }
"""


y1=np.random.multivariate_normal([7,9],[[1,0.8],[0.8,2]],size=50)
y2=np.random.multivariate_normal([15,17],[[2,0.1],[0.1,2]],size=150)
y=np.random.permutation(np.concatenate((y1,y2)))

mix_dat = {   'N': len(y),
             'D':2,
             'K':2,
             'alpha':np.array([1,1]),
              'y': y}



fit = pystan.stan(model_code=mix_code, data=mix_dat,
                 iter=500, chains=1)

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Finite Mixture of Multivariate Normals
parts:
Could someone else other than me take a look at this and
see if you can see anything wrong --- it looks properly
coded and the data generation looks OK to me, so I don't see why it's
not working. Thanks.

(If I get some time, I'll try to write one of my own from
scratch and see if I can get it working.)

Stan should certainly be able to fit such a model. Lots
of people have implemented mixtures of varying components.

If you don't plan to generalize beyond two components, I'd
recommend simplifying to a beta prior, using log(theta) and
log1m(theta) and the two-argument log_sum_exp, or even better,
the new log_mix() function. But that shouldn't be the problem.

You also want to change this:

> transformed parameters{
> matrix[D,D] var_cov[K];
> for (m in 1:K){
> var_cov[m] <- diag_pre_multiply(tau[m],L_Omega[m]) * diag_pre_multiply(tau[m],L_Omega[m])';
> }
> }

There is a multiply_self_transpose() function that's much more
efficient than using diag_pre_mulitply twice. But
if you're going to use a Cholesky parameterization, you can
just go all the way and use multi_normal_cholesky. But again, this
is just an efficiency issue.

If you have a dirichlet(1) prior, you can just drop it. The
default is a uniform prior over the parameters as declared (here
that'd be uniform over simplexes). Again, just an efficiency issue.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Finite Mixture of Multivariate Normals
parts:
I'm afraid I don't really speak Python, but I could understand
what you're doing and recreate it in R. I didn't try to debug
what you did, but I'm attaching our recommended approach to
dealing with multivariate normals along with some simulation
code in R that successfully fits the mixture.

Here's the Stan program, which I just hardcoded to two
mixture components.


mix.stan
-----------------------------------------------
data {
int<lower=0> N;
int<lower=1> D;
vector[D] y[N];
}
parameters {
real<lower=0,upper=1> theta;
vector[D] mu[2];
cholesky_factor_corr[D] L_Omega[2];
vector<lower=0>[D] sigma[2];
}
transformed parameters {
cholesky_factor_cov[D] L_Sigma[2];
for (k in 1:2)
L_Sigma[k] <- diag_pre_multiply(sigma[k], L_Omega[k]);
}
model {
theta ~ beta(1,1);
for (k in 1:2) {
sigma[k] ~ cauchy(0,2);
L_Omega[k] ~ lkj_corr_cholesky(1);
mu[k] ~ normal(0,5);
}
for (n in 1:N) {
real lp1;
real lp2;
lp1 <- multi_normal_cholesky_log(y[n], mu[1], L_Sigma[1]);
lp2 <- multi_normal_cholesky_log(y[n], mu[2], L_Sigma[2]);
increment_log_prob(log_sum_exp(log(theta) + lp1,
log1m(theta) + lp2));
}
}
generated quantities {
cov_matrix[D] Sigma[2];
for (k in 1:2)
Sigma[k] <- multiply_lower_tri_self_transpose(L_Sigma[k]);
}
-----------------------------------------

This works out to uniform priors on the mixture ratio theta and
also on the correlation matrices.


Here's the simulator, using same parameters as Vasileios, but more
data:


sim.R
-----------------------------------
library(MASS);

mu1 <- c(7,9);
Sigma1 <- matrix(c(1, 0.8, 0.8, 2), 2, 2);

mu2 <- c(15,17);
Sigma2 <- matrix(c(2, 0.1, 0.1, 2), 2, 2);

y <- rbind(mvrnorm(200,mu1,Sigma1), mvrnorm(600,mu2,Sigma2));
N <- dim(y)[1]
D <- 2;
-------------------------------

Note that it's four times as many samples. Covariance
matrices are notoriously difficult to estimate. If you
use the data sizes you started with, the covariances won't
even be as well estimated as they are with 200 and 600 data
points.


Here's the code to run it in R:

fit.R
-----------------------------------------
library(rstan);

fit <- stan("mix.stan", data=c("N","D","y"),
control=list(stepsize=0.001),
chains=1, iter=1000,
seed = 7654321);
------------------------------------------


Note that I set the initial stepsize to 0.001. This is often a good
idea in complex models to cut down on Hamiltonian simulation errors early
in warmup.
mean se_mean sd 2.5% 25% 50% 75% 97.5% n_eff Rhat

theta 0.25 0.00 0.01 0.23 0.24 0.25 0.26 0.28 430 1

mu[1,1] 7.06 0.00 0.08 6.92 7.01 7.06 7.12 7.20 377 1

Sigma[1,1,2] 0.84 0.01 0.12 0.61 0.77 0.85 0.92 1.09 390 1
Sigma[1,2,1] 0.84 0.01 0.12 0.61 0.77 0.85 0.92 1.09 390 1

That's not bad, but you can see that the posterior on the covariance terms
is still fairly wide.

What I would suggest you do going forward is modify this code to use
the Dirichlet and make sure you get the same answer with two components.
Then generalize to more components.

Then you could enrich other parts of it. But it's best to leave everything
parameterized as is using the Cholesky factors.

In Stan 2.6, if you only need two components, you should replace

increment_log_prob(log_sum_exp(log(theta) + lp1,
log1m(theta) + lp2));

with

increment_log_prob(log_mix(theta, lp1, lp2));

- Bob

> of people have implemented mixtures of varying components.
>
> If you don't plan to generalize beyond two components, I'd
> recommend simplifying to a beta prior, using log(theta) and
> log1m(theta) and the two-argument log_sum_exp, or even better,

> efficient than using diag_pre_mulitply twice. But

>
> If you have a dirichlet(1) prior, you can just drop it. The

Dear Bob,

Your R-script runs like a charm and apparently using more data in my python code seems to work as well. I 'll check whether something funny goes on with the numerical precisions in python.

I want to use HMC in order to fit a finite mixture model in which the distributions are not from the same family and 1 of them is parametrised for that specific problem. So, I came across Stan as an alternative to writing my own code. 

However, I have been trying to fit a simple finite mixture model for multivariate Normals but I am clearly missing something. More specifically, I simulate some data from 2 distributions and one of the mixing parameters goes to 1 and the other to 0 every time I run the script. The code with the generated data is the following:



mix_code="""

   int<lower=0> N; // number of individuals

   cholesky_factor_corr[D] L_Omega[K];
   vector<lower=0>[D] tau[K];

  transformed parameters{

   for (m in 1:K){
     var_cov[m] <- diag_pre_multiply(tau[m],L_Omega[m]) * diag_pre_multiply(tau[m],L_Omega[m])';
   }
 }
 

  model {
   real ps[K];
   theta ~ dirichlet(alpha);
   for(m in 1:K) {
     // Priors for var-cov matrices and mu:
     tau[m] ~ cauchy(0,5);
     L_Omega[m] ~ lkj_corr_cholesky(D);
     mu[m]~normal(0,10);
   }
   
   for(n in 1:N) {
     for(m in 1:K) {
       ps[m] <- log(theta[m]) + multi_normal_log(y[n],mu[m],var_cov[m]);
     }
     increment_log_prob(log_sum_exp(ps));
   }
